Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Two years ago, while on a work assignment in a region simmering with ethnic tension, Maya witnessed a fire engulf a cluster of Arab-owned shops. She heard the screams, the crackling, the shouts. She stood frozen, unable to move, watching as flames consumed the building. In the aftermath, she learned that several people had died. She was unharmed, but the image of the fire and the sounds haunted her. Back home, Maya tried to return to her life as a data scientist, but the world felt different. A news report about tensions in the Middle East would send her heart racing; the smell of a barbecue grill from a neighbor's yard could trigger a full flashback - suddenly she was back there, hearing the screams, feeling the heat. These triggers made her feel threatened by strangers, especially men of certain ethnicities, even in ordinary situations like walking to her car. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found that even ordinary sounds - a car backfiring, a door slamming - now carried a charge that made her heart pound. She started checking doors and locks repeatedly, a habit she couldn't shake. The same triggers also stirred her deepest guilt: she became convinced that she should have done something - that she had failed to protect those people. She would compare herself to others, thinking that someone braver would have rushed in to help. These negative appraisals made the memories feel more real than her everyday life; the auditory fragments of screams and fire seemed to echo inside her head without warning, and then the memories themselves would bring back the guilt more sharply. Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in the way certain smells carried her back, in the faces of strangers who reminded her of the crowd that day. To cope with the constant threat and the intrusive memories, Maya threw herself into her work, taking on extra projects and working late into the night. She found that if she kept her mind occupied with data, she could avoid being alone with her thoughts. But the ruminations came anyway - she would go over and over why this event had happened to her, as if searching for a meaning that never arrived. This overwork and rumination, in turn, kept the memories vivid and easily triggered, because she was never really resting. The stress of her long hours itself became a new trigger, and the exhaustion made her feel even more vulnerable to the threat of strangers. Once the flashback had taken hold, the threat felt immediate and physical - not something that had happened, but something that was still unfolding around her. She began checking locks more obsessively after a late night at the office, certain that someone might be outside. Her husband noticed she was distant, spending hours in her home office, and when she did come to bed, she would lie awake, alert, replaying the sounds. The more she worked, the more her memories intruded, and the more she felt she had failed - a self-reinforcing loop that left her sleeping only a few hours a night. Eventually, Maya found herself unable to focus on the data she once loved. She had started to wonder if her life was worth living anymore, a thought that frightened her enough to mention it to her husband. It was he who finally insisted she seek help. Now, sitting in a therapist's office, Maya is most afraid that talking about what happened will make the memories even more real - and what she hopes for, though she can barely admit it, is a way to stop the cycle without losing herself completely.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory leads to a sense of threat; the vignette only shows triggers causing threat, not memory.
No paragraph conveys that the memory itself becomes or creates triggers; only stress from overwork becomes a trigger.
No paragraph conveys that feeling threatened leads to new triggers; the causal direction is only from triggers to threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory leads to a sense of threat; the vignette only shows triggers causing threat, not memory.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself becomes or creates triggers; only stress from overwork becomes a trigger.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that feeling threatened leads to new triggers; the causal direction is only from triggers to threat.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
